meta.description: No — Benjamin Franklin never said it. This antimetabole traces to psychologist G. Stanley Hall (1904), not a 1700s founding father. Here’s the paper trail.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We do not stop playing because we grow old; we grow old because we stop playing'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Benjamin Franklin. The thought traces to psychologist G. Stanley Hall in 1904, evolving from Karl Groos (1896). Franklin died in 1790.

answer.label: Not Benjamin Franklin — a 20th-century saying, closest to psychologist G. Stanley Hall
answer.authorDates: 1844–1924 · American psychologist · pioneer of the study of adolescence
answer.sourceLine: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) never said this — it is not in his writings and post-dates him by well over a century. The oldest documented English form is psychologist G. Stanley Hall’s in Adolescence (1904): “men grow old because they stop playing, and not conversely.” Per Quote Investigator, the neat mirror-image (antimetabole) wording emerged around 1908–1909; the polished modern sentence is an anonymous later crystallization, not a Franklin line.

source.heading: Where the saying actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Karl Groos, The Play of Animals (1896/1898 trans.)
Evolved aphorism (antimetabole); no single fixed author
Benjamin Franklin, G. B. Shaw, Herbert Spencer, O. W. Holmes

source.excerpt: “men grow old because they stop playing, and not conversely” — G. Stanley Hall, Adolescence (1904). By 1908 George L. Knapp had cast the idea as a mirror-image: “We do not so much quit playing because we grow old, as grow old because we quit playing.”
trail: Quote Investigator traces the thought to Karl Groos (1896) and its first English form to psychologist G. Stanley Hall in Adolescence (1904); the mirror-image phrasing appears by 1908–1909.
QI records credits to Herbert Spencer (1915), George Bernard Shaw (1983), and Oliver Wendell Holmes — and finds “no compelling supporting evidence” for any of them.

The Benjamin Franklin credit is a purely modern web phenomenon: it appears on aggregators like Goodreads with no source, and Franklin (d. 1790) predates every documented instance by more than a century.
source.excerptNote: The tidy modern wording — “We do not stop playing because we grow old; we grow old because we stop playing” — is a smoothed, anonymous descendant of these early-1900s formulations, not a verbatim quotation from any one author.
source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording is an anonymous 20th-century crystallization with no single identifiable first-publication, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. The documented early variants — Hall’s 1904 Adolescence and Knapp’s 1908 article — are themselves public domain, but they are worded differently from the line shown here.

author.name: G. Stanley Hall
author.heading: The psychologist behind the idea
author.metaLine: 1844–1924 · American psychologist · founder of the American Psychological Association
author.bio: Granville Stanley Hall was a pioneering American psychologist and educator, the first president of the American Psychological Association and of Clark University. His two-volume Adolescence (1904) popularized the study of youth and contained the earliest English form of the play-and-aging idea — “men grow old because they stop playing” — which he adapted from Karl Groos. The polished modern proverb is a later, anonymous reworking of that thought, and has nothing to do with Benjamin Franklin.

misattribution.heading: A magnet for famous names
misattribution.intro: This feel-good aphorism has been pinned on a rotating cast of celebrated men — none of whom can be shown to have written it. It is a textbook “orphan proverb” that acquires a prestigious signature to travel farther.

items.why: Franklin (1706–1790) died more than a century before any version of this saying is documented. It appears in none of his works and is absent from serious Franklin scholarship; Quote Investigator does not even list him among the claimants. The credit is a modern aggregator invention seen on sites like Goodreads.

items.who: George Bernard Shaw, Herbert Spencer, Oliver Wendell Holmes
items.why: QI documents credits to Herbert Spencer (1915), George Bernard Shaw (1983), and Oliver Wendell Holmes, and concludes there is “no compelling supporting evidence” for any of them.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is real and old — it runs from Karl Groos (1896) through psychologist G. Stanley Hall (1904) — but the polished modern sentence has no single author, and Benjamin Franklin is not one of the candidates.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Franklin
lead: The line is built as an antimetabole — the same words flipped (“stop playing / grow old” → “grow old / stop playing”) — a rhetorical shape that feels aphoristic and quotable. Franklin’s reputation as America’s pithy sage makes him a low-friction host for any snappy maxim about living well, which is exactly how orphan sayings end up under his name.

In reality the idea belongs to turn-of-the-century psychology of play: Karl Groos argued animals have a youth because they play, and G. Stanley Hall turned that into a claim about human aging. The Franklin signature is decoration added a century later.
context.pull: The thought is Hall’s and Groos’s; the Franklin byline is decoration added a century later.
